title_en: Shi Wenpei v. Gansu Huangtai Brewing (Group) Co., Ltd. and Beijing Huangtai Commerce and Trade Co., Ltd. — dispute over a barter contract
ruling_gist_en: 1. Although two contracts signed between the parties involve the same batch of goods, since the purposes and agreed contents of the two contracts are different, the value of the goods shall be determined respectively in accordance with the terms of each contract, and the relevant stipulations on the value of the goods in one contract cannot be negated by the stipulations in the other contract.
keywords_en: Civil; Barter contract dispute; Second instance; Supreme People's Court; Gansu Province; Beijing Municipality; Natural person; Legal person; Contract Law; Determination of contractually agreed value of goods; Conditions for adjustment of excessive liquidated damages; Whether liquidated damages should be adjusted in case of bad faith breach; Partially sustained; Barter contract; Liquor barter; Alcohol delivery; Company name change; Dispute over liquidated damages; Good faith; Contract dispute; Arbitration; Barter contract dispute of a limited liability company
full_text_en:
Shi Wenpei v. Gansu Huangtai Brewing (Group) Co., Ltd.
and Beijing Huangtai Commerce & Trade Co., Ltd.
— Dispute over Barter Contract

[Ruling Summary]

I. Although the two contracts executed between the parties concerned the same batch of goods, because the purposes and agreed content of the two contracts were different, the value of the goods should be determined separately according to the respective contracts, and the agreement on the value of the goods in one contract cannot negate the relevant agreement in the other contract.

II. Under Article 114, paragraph 2 of the Contract Law, a party may request the People's Court or an arbitral institution to appropriately reduce the liquidated damages only when the agreed liquidated damages are excessively higher than the losses actually caused. Therefore, in the case of a party's malicious breach of contract, if there is no evidence proving that the agreed liquidated damages are excessively higher than the losses actually caused, the People's Court may not support the party's request to reduce the liquidated damages.

Supreme People's Court
Civil Judgment

(2007) Min Er Zhong Zi No. 139

Appellant (Defendant at First Instance): Gansu Huangtai Brewing (Group) Co., Ltd., domiciled at No. 55 Xinjian Road, Wuwei City, Gansu Province.

Legal Representative: Zhang Jingfa, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Gao Weipeng, lawyer of Beijing Shilian Xinjiyuan Law Firm.

Appellee (Plaintiff at First Instance): Shi Wenpei, male, Han nationality, born on May 31, 1960, residing at Room 5, Gate No. 1, No. 7 Nanbaxi Road, Tiexi District, Shenyang City, Liaoning Province.

Agent ad litem: Cai Yongmin, lawyer of Gansu Tianma Law Firm.

Defendant at First Instance: Beijing Huangtai Commerce & Trade Co., Ltd., domiciled at Room 1018, Block K, Huiyuan International Apartment, Yayun Village, No. 8 Beichen East Road, Chaoyang District, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Wang Guoyi, Chairman of the Board.

The appellant Gansu Huangtai Brewing (Group) Co., Ltd. appealed to this Court against the civil judgment (2007) Gan Min Er Chu Zi No. 01 rendered by the Gansu High People's Court in the dispute over a barter contract with the appellee Shi Wenpei and the defendant at first instance Beijing Huangtai Commerce & Trade Co., Ltd. This Court lawfully formed a collegial panel composed of Presiding Judge Ye Xiaoqing, Judge Chen Mingyan, and Judge Wang Chuang to conduct a hearing. Clerk Zhang Yongshu served as the court recorder for this case. The trial of this case has now been concluded.

The court of first instance found the following facts upon trial:

On July 6, 2002, Gansu Huangtai Brewing (Group) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Gansu Huangtai), as Party A, entered into a "Barter Agreement" with Beijing Jianhao Industrial Company (hereinafter referred to as Jianhao Industrial), as Party B, which stated: "Parties A and B entered into an 'Agreement' in 1998, whereby Party B purchased from Party A 'Jin Huangtai' and 'Yin Huangtai' liquor valued at RMB 7 million. Party A has delivered all the goods to Party B, and Party B has paid the purchase price in full. Now, Party B offers to exchange the unsold portion of the aforesaid liquor at the time of execution of this Agreement with Party A for edible alcohol and wine sold by Party A. Considering the long-term cooperative relationship with Party B, Party A agrees to Party B's barter request. The parties, after negotiation and mutual agreement, have reached the following agreement: 1. The liquor used to barter for edible alcohol and wine from Party A must be the 'Jin Huangtai' and 'Yin Huangtai' liquor purchased by Party B from Party A under the aforesaid liquor purchase and sale contract that remains unsold at the time of execution of this Agreement, and such liquor must have intact inner and outer packaging. After both parties jointly inspected the inventory at Party B's warehouse, the value of the liquor to be bartered was determined to be RMB 6,499,500. Party A agrees to provide Party B with edible alcohol and wine of equivalent value under this Agreement. 2. The parties agree that on the date of execution of this Agreement, Party A shall transfer the aforesaid liquor from Party B's warehouse to Party A's warehouse. At the time of transfer, the parties shall sign a goods (liquor) transfer record, noting the content and quantity of the goods received by Party A. 3. The varieties and prices of edible alcohol and wine to be bartered by Party A to Party B are: Premium Edible Alcohol at RMB 4,500 per ton; Huangtai Dry Red Wine at RMB 20 per bottle. The parties agree on the quantities of edible alcohol and wine to be exchanged: 75,000 bottles of Huangtai Dry Red Wine, totaling RMB 1.5 million, and 1,111 tons of Premium Edible Alcohol, totaling RMB 4,999,500. 4. Party A shall deliver all the wine on the date of liquor transfer, and the edible alcohol shall be delivered before December 31, 2003. If Party A fails to deliver the alcohol within this period, it shall bear liquidated damages at the rate of 0.04% per day of the value of the delayed delivery. 6. Except for the barter arrangement for edible alcohol as provided in this Agreement, without Party A's consent, Party B may not require Party A to pay in monetary form or by other means the value of the liquor returned by Party B to Party A." From September 13 to September 20, 2002, Beijing Huangtai Commerce & Trade Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Beijing Huangtai) received the "Jin Huangtai" liquor and issued a receipt to Jianhao Industrial. On May 12, 2003, Jianhao Industrial sent a letter to Gansu Huangtai stating: "Our party is ready to receive the alcohol. Please contact us as soon as possible regarding shipment." The letter bore the seal of Jianhao Industrial. On May 16, 2003, Gansu Huangtai replied to Jianhao Industrial (Group) Company, stating: "Due to the current impact of the 'SARS' epidemic, transportation of edible goods is restricted, combined with difficulties in allocating specialized railway transport tanks, we are unable to ship the goods to your company as scheduled. Once the epidemic subsides, we will deliver the goods to your company in full." On June 7, 2003, Gansu Huangtai replied to Jianhao Industrial (Group) Company, stating: "We have received your letter of June 2, 'Another Letter to Huangtai Liquor Industry Regarding the Issue of Alcohol Delivery.' Because railway regulations do not permit the consignment of flammable and explosive goods, our company is unable to meet your requirement for delivery of alcohol by rail transport." On May 31, 2004, Gansu Huangtai sent a letter to Jianhao Industrial stating: "After our company signed the barter agreement with your company, our company performed its contractual obligations according to the agreement. However, there were rumors that Yuan Baojing was involved in a criminal case and had his personal freedom restricted. At the same time, different individuals, including senior employees of your company, relatives of the legal representative, and other persons, made different demands to our company in the name of your company regarding the performance of the barter agreement. Since our company is unaware whether Yuan Baojing still performs the duties of legal representative of your company and whether your company has undergone an adjustment in corporate power, our company cannot rashly accept the demands of the aforesaid persons, and of course, this also prevents our company from continuing to perform the contractual obligations. Recently, we also received a lawyer's letter from a person authorized by your company regarding the performance of the barter agreement. Our company hereby writes to your company: 1. If your company has authorized relevant persons to negotiate with our company regarding the performance of the barter agreement, please inform our company by letter so that our company can confirm the authorized persons. 2. Whether the authorization of relevant persons by your company is lawful and whether the acts of the authorized persons can represent your company shall be the responsibility of your company and the relevant persons, who shall bear the legal consequences arising therefrom. Our company shall not be liable." On June 3, 2004, Beijing Jianhao Investment Group Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Jianhao Investment) sent a letter to Gansu Huangtai titled "Letter Regarding the Barter Agreement," stating: "We have received your letter. We respond to your concerns as follows: 1. Our company's former legal representative Yuan Baojing is temporarily not serving as legal representative; the current legal representative has been changed to Ms. Tang Zeying. Even if our company does not change the legal representative, it does not affect the performance of this agreement. 2. Jianhao Industrial has been approved by the Beijing Administration for Industry and Commerce to change its name to Jianhao Investment Group Co., Ltd. 3. At your company's request, our company has now formally authorized our Deputy General Manager Liao Yanxian to fully handle all matters related to the barter agreement entered into with your company. For the convenience of work, please designate the relevant departments and personnel to contact us as soon as possible and cooperate with us. If your company fails to perform its obligations and responsibilities under the barter agreement, following the advice of our company's lawyers, we reserve the right to resolve the issue through other means to protect our company's lawful rights and interests." On June 4, 2004, Gansu Huangtai sent a letter to Jianhao Investment stating: "The barter agreement was entered into between our company and Jianhao Industrial, and thereafter, persons who requested negotiations with our company regarding the barter agreement also acted in the name of Jianhao Industrial. In the two years from the signing of the barter agreement to the present, our company has only now learned of the change of company name. We hope your company can provide certification from the Administration for Industry and Commerce regarding the name change. Upon verification, our company will promptly contact your company." On July 17, 2004, Gansu Huangtai sent a letter to Jianhao Investment stating: "Your company informed our company that Jianhao Industrial had changed its name and requested our company to perform the barter agreement to your company. However, based on the materials provided by your company regarding the name change, by the time our company signed the barter agreement with Jianhao Industrial, the company had already changed its name. It is difficult to understand that a company would still use its old name to enter into contracts with others after the name change. Moreover, the explanation from your company's senior management that 'due to time constraints and incomplete procedures, the new seal could not be used' is inconsistent with the fact that the name change had already been in place for half a year, as evidenced by the materials provided by your company. At the same time, our company has recently received lawyer's letters separately from 'Jianhao Industrial' and from your company as the client. Whether your company still uses the old name or there are other reasons, the barter agreement was signed personally between our company's legal representative and Yuan Baojing. Our company looks forward to a face-to-face meeting with Yuan Baojing for friendly negotiation."

On September 20, 2005, Jianhao Investment (Party A) and the plaintiff Shi Wenpei (Party B) entered into an "Assignment Agreement for Creditor's Rights," which stated: "1. Party A agrees to assign to Party B the creditor's rights against Gansu Huangtai for high-quality edible alcohol valued at RMB 5 million and interest thereon. All rights and obligations enjoyed or undertaken by Party A under the 'Agreement' and 'Barter Agreement' entered into with Gansu Huangtai are transferred to Party B. 2. Party B accepts the aforesaid creditor's rights of Party A. 3. Party A shall not revoke the aforesaid creditor's rights without Party B's consent." On September 21, Jianhao Investment delivered a "Notice of Assignment of Creditor's Rights" to Gansu Huangtai, which stated: "Gansu Huangtai, the creditor's rights for edible alcohol valued at RMB 4,999,500 and the interest accrued thereon that our company has against your company are now assigned to Shi Wenpei. Shi Wenpei will enjoy all of our company's said creditor's rights against your company." The notice bore the signature "Jianhao Investment (formerly Beijing Jianhao Industrial Company)." On September 30, 2004, Gansu Huangtai sent a letter to Jianhao Investment stating: "We have received your company's 'Notice of Assignment of Creditor's Rights' of September 21. We hereby respond as follows: 1. Your company previously stated that your company was formed from the name change of Jianhao Industrial. However, the documents provided by your company confirm that the barter agreement entered into between our company and Jianhao Industrial was executed after your company's name change. Therefore, the party to the agreement remains Jianhao Industrial, and the creditor-debtor relationship and amounts arising from the barter agreement can only be confirmed between our company and Jianhao Industrial. Your company has no right to claim it holds a creditor's right of RMB 4,999,500 against our company. 2. Based on the foregoing facts, your company's assignment of the alleged creditor's rights against our company to Shi Wenpei will cause adverse effects on our company and damage our company's image. We hope your company will take immediate measures to prevent the further spread of adverse effects."

It was also found that Jianhao Industrial was established in October 1992, organized by the Jinjian Labor Service Company of the People's Construction Bank of China, approved by the Huairou County Planning Commission, with a registered capital of RMB 1 million, as a collectively-owned enterprise, with the legal representative being Yuan Jingmin. On November 21, 2001, Jianhao Industrial changed its name to Beijing Jianhao Investment Group Co., Ltd., with the enterprise type changed to a limited liability company, through overall restructuring. On December 7, 2001, the business license of Jianhao Investment was issued, with a registered capital of RMB 100 million, the legal representative being Yuan Jingmin, holding 20% shares, and shareholder Yuan Baojing holding 80% shares. On April 15, 2002, the resolution of the shareholders' meeting of Jianhao Investment was affixed with the seal of Jianhao Investment. The following day, the authorization letter for enterprise change registration also bore the seal of Jianhao Investment.

It was also found that the registered capital of Beijing Huangtai was RMB 362 million; apart from contributions of RMB 3.86 million by Beijing Shengshi Hengchang Commerce & Trade Co., Ltd. and RMB 4 million by Beijing Shengshi Ruilong Advertising Co., Ltd., the remainder consisted of contributions by Gansu Huangtai in the form of assets and equity.

On November 21, 2006, Shi Wenpei filed a lawsuit with the Gansu High People's Court, requesting a judgment ordering Gansu Huangtai and Beijing Huangtai to pay the owed 1,111 tons of edible alcohol (valued at RMB 4,999,500), and to bear liability for breach of contract and losses totaling RMB 11 million, and to bear all litigation costs.

The Gansu High People's Court held upon trial that the barter agreement was entered into by Gansu Huangtai and Jianhao Industrial on July 6, 2002. The content of the contract represented the true intention of both parties, did not violate legal provisions, and therefore should be recognized as a valid contract. Although Jianhao Investment had already been established when the contract was signed, given that the contract was actually performed, and that Gansu Huangtai referred to Jianhao Industrial as Jianhao Industrial (Group) Company in correspondence during the performance of the contract, it should be recognized that Gansu Huangtai knew of the name change of Jianhao Industrial and did not raise any objection. The fact that Gansu Huangtai disputed the proper party to the contract with Jianhao Investment due to the name change of Jianhao Industrial and the change of legal representative did not affect the validity of the contract. Since Jianhao Investment was formed through the restructuring of Jianhao Industrial, there was a legal succession relationship, and Yuan Baojing had never served as the legal representative of either Jianhao Industrial or Jianhao Investment, but only as a shareholder of the company. Therefore, Gansu Huangtai should perform its obligations to Jianhao Investment. Jianhao Investment assigned the creditor's rights to the plaintiff Shi Wenpei and notified the debtor Gansu Huangtai. This assignment did not violate legal provisions and should be valid. Shi Wenpei is the proper party to this case. Although the assigned creditor's right in the assignment agreement was stated as edible alcohol valued at RMB 5 million and corresponding interest, the notice to Gansu Huangtai clearly informed of a creditor's right of RMB 4,999,500, and the assignment agreement did not include the assignment of obligations. Gansu Huangtai's defenses lacked factual and legal basis and could not be sustained; the court did not adopt them. Because Gansu Huangtai failed to deliver the alcohol within the contractual delivery time, it breached the contract, and should bear liability for breach and the obligation to continue performance. The plaintiff's claim for rights based on the quantity and value of alcohol agreed in the contract and the liability for breach was legally grounded and should be supported by the court. Regarding the losses claimed by the plaintiff, as the plaintiff only provided materials regarding the appraisal of Jinshishan Hotel at No. 4 Longshan East Road, Huairou District, Beijing, and some materials regarding the auction of that hotel by the Beijing No. 2 Intermediate People's Court, which could not prove that the losses were caused by the non-performance of the barter contract in this case, the claim for losses was not supported due to insufficient evidence. Regarding the relationship between Beijing Huangtai and this case, since the "Barter Agreement" was signed by Gansu Huangtai and Jianhao Industrial, Beijing Huangtai's receipt of goods and issuance of receipt to Jianhao Industrial was only an act on behalf of Gansu Huangtai, and Beijing Huangtai did not participate in the performance of the contract or in the correspondence, nor did Beijing Huangtai appear in the notice of assignment of creditor's rights. This sufficiently proves that Beijing Huangtai was not a party to the contract. Beijing Huangtai's defense was valid and was adopted by the court. In accordance with Article 85 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC, Articles 79, 80, 114(1)(3), and 175 of the Contract Law of the PRC, the court ordered: 1. Gansu Huangtai shall continue to perform its obligation to supply 1,111 tons of alcohol under the barter agreement to Shi Wenpei, or pay compensation of equivalent value in the amount of RMB 4,999,500; 2. Gansu Huangtai shall pay to Shi Wenpei liquidated damages totaling RMB 2,099,790; 3. The lawsuit against Beijing Huangtai is dismissed. The payment obligations under paragraphs 1 and 2 above shall be performed within 15 days after this judgment takes effect. In case of delayed performance, the debt shall be doubled as interest for the period of delayed performance in accordance with Article 232 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC. Court acceptance fee of RMB 78,012 and preservation fee of RMB 5,000, totaling RMB 83,012, shall be borne by Gansu Huangtai.

Appellant Gansu Huangtai appealed to this Court against the civil judgment of the Gansu High People's Court, alleging: First, the first instance judgment's determination that Jianhao Investment was derived from the restructuring of Jianhao Industry, and therefore had a legal succession relationship, was difficult to sustain. Jianhao Industry was a collectively-owned enterprise established by the Jinshang Service Company of the People's Construction Bank of China. Jianhao Investment was a limited liability company registered on December 7, 2001, with shareholders Yuan Jingmin and Yuan Baojing. The original founding entity, Jinshang Service Company, was not a shareholder. Jianhao Investment was established entirely according to the procedures and conditions for new company formation under the Company Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Company Law). Its registration was a change in registration in form but a new registration in substance. The so-called restructuring was merely Yuan Baojing and Yuan Jingmin purchasing the assets of Jianhao Industry and using them as personal capital contributions to establish Jianhao Investment. The two enterprises had no connection or succession relationship; the only relationship was an irregular registration by the industrial and commercial authorities, which recorded it as a restructuring and allowed a name change registration. The first instance judgment, without examining the relationship between the two enterprises under the Company Law, arbitrarily determined a restructuring based on erroneous industrial and commercial registration and then found a legal succession relationship, which was unsustainable. Second, Jianhao Industry was not qualified as a party to the barter contract and could not enjoy the rights and obligations under that contract. Even if Jianhao Investment was derived from the restructuring of Jianhao Industry, with a legal succession relationship, the trade agreement signed by Yuan Baojing in the name of Jianhao Industry with the appellant was entered into by Yuan Baojing using the name of Jianhao Industry, which had already been legally terminated. Pursuant to Article 49 of the Several Opinions of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the party B to the barter agreement signed by Yuan Baojing in the name of Jianhao Industry should be Yuan Baojing individually, and the rights and obligations under the contract should also belong to Yuan Baojing individually. Jianhao Industry did not have the qualification as a party to the barter contract, and Jianhao Investment could not naturally succeed to the rights and obligations of the barter contract by legally succeeding Jianhao Industry. Jianhao Investment's notice of performance and transfer of rights and obligations under the barter contract constituted unauthorized disposition and should be deemed invalid pursuant to Article 51 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Contract Law). Third, the first instance judgment's finding that Gansu Huangtai breached the contract lacked factual basis. In the barter agreement, the parties did not clearly stipulate the place and method of delivery for Gansu Huangtai's delivery of wine. Since Gansu Huangtai entrusted Beijing Huangtai to store some of the wine, during contract performance, Gansu Huangtai delivered the wine at Beijing Huangtai's warehouse in order to facilitate the realization of the contract purpose. However, regarding the edible alcohol, at the time of signing, Yuan Baojing was well aware that the subject matter was in Wuwei, Gansu. According to Article 62, Paragraph 1, Item 3 of the Contract Law, delivery should take place at the location of Gansu Huangtai, i.e., Wuwei, Gansu. During performance, the method most conducive to achieving the contract purpose should have been for Yuan Baojing to come to Wuwei to accept delivery. During performance, Gansu Huangtai, out of consideration for providing assistance, contacted railway transportation on multiple occasions, but was unsuccessful because the railway did not handle flammable and explosive goods. Gansu Huangtai truthfully informed Yuan Baojing of this situation and requested him to come to Wuwei to accept delivery. Yuan Baojing never came to take delivery. Subsequently, when Jianhao Investment asserted its rights, due to disputes between the parties, Jianhao Investment was unable to provide proof from the rights holder Yuan Baojing. Jianhao Investment's rights were in a pending confirmation status, and Yuan Baojing was in custody, making it impossible for Gansu Huangtai to contact or urge him to take delivery, resulting in the failure to deliver. Meanwhile, Jianhao Investment raised no objection to the delayed delivery. The first instance judgment, without examining the unclear stipulations on the place and method of contract performance, arbitrarily concluded that Gansu Huangtai should have delivered in Beijing and had breached the contract, which lacked factual basis. Fourth, even if Beijing Huangtai received the liquor delivered by Jianhao Investment, based on the 16 receipts provided by Shi Wenpei and the liquor prices stipulated in the 1998 Agreement between Jianhao Investment and Gansu Huangtai, the value of the liquor delivered by Jianhao Investment was only RMB 4,328,340, not the RMB 6,499,500 agreed upon in the Barter Agreement. Furthermore, Gansu Huangtai could not prove its actual losses, and the liquidated damages stipulated in the Barter Agreement were clearly excessive. If Gansu Huangtai should bear liquidated damages, the proportion of liquidated damages should be reduced pursuant to Article 114 of the Contract Law. Therefore, Shi Wenpei's claim that Gansu Huangtai should pay him RMB 4,999,500 and liquidated damages was untenable. In summary, the appellant requested that the second instance court set aside the first instance judgment and dismiss Shi Wenpei's claims.

The appellee, Shi Wenpei, argued: The first instance court's findings of fact were clear and the evidence was sufficient. First, regarding the issue that Jianhao Investment was derived from the restructuring of Jianhao Industry and had a legal succession relationship, this was evidenced by the enterprise restructuring registration certificate and the enterprise name pre-approval notice, and further corroborated by a certificate issued by the Beijing Administration for Industry and Commerce. Whether viewed from the perspective of the constitutive or declaratory effect of enterprise industrial and commercial registration, the succession relationship was proved. Gansu Huangtai's assertion that the industrial and commercial registration was irregular or erroneous was entirely unfounded. It was not for Gansu Huangtai to conclude whether the enterprise restructuring was lawful or standardized. If Gansu Huangtai believed that the industrial and commercial administration had infringed its rights, it could sue the industrial and commercial administration department. Second, Gansu Huangtai's grounds for appeal only examined superficial issues and failed to provide any valid evidence. It was well known that the establishment and alteration of an enterprise were based on industrial and commercial registration (or change of registration) as the benchmark for enjoying rights and undertaking obligations externally. Where was Gansu Huangtai's basis for claiming that Jianhao Investment was re-established in accordance with the Company Law? Third, regarding Gansu Huangtai's assertion that Yuan Baojing used the name of Jianhao Industry improperly, from the signing of the agreement to its performance and up to the correspondence urging delivery of the remaining alcohol, all transactions occurred between Jianhao Industry or its successor, Jianhao Investment, and Gansu Huangtai. At no time did Yuan Baojing claim performance in his individual capacity, nor did Gansu Huangtai ever raise an issue regarding the improper subject of the contract. Gansu Huangtai's sudden raising of the subject issue during litigation could only be interpreted as an attempt to evade debts. From the signing of the contract to its actual performance, it was always carried out in the name of Jianhao Industry. How could it be said that Jianhao Industry was not qualified as a party to the barter contract? Jianhao Investment's claim for rights against Gansu Huangtai was also because it succeeded Jianhao Industry. Since there was a legal succession relationship, it naturally had the right to assert claims against Gansu Huangtai. The subject of the barter contract was the enterprise, not an individual. As long as the relationship between them could be proved, there was no need to provide Yuan Baojing's individual proof. Moreover, in the correspondence, the appellee knew it was corporate conduct, not individual conduct, and the correspondence consistently referred to commitments made by the company, not Yuan Baojing individually. Finally, regarding the issue of contract breach. From the time Jianhao Industry began urging Gansu Huangtai to deliver the alcohol, Gansu Huangtai continuously made excuses such as SARS making railway transportation unsuitable, preparing to purchase special equipment for vehicle delivery, and the railway's refusal to handle flammable and explosive goods. However, it never actually requested Jianhao Industry to take delivery, specifying neither a specific time nor a specific place. The facts of the breach existed, and Gansu Huangtai should bear liability for breach. In summary, Gansu Huangtai's claims violated the principle of good faith, were contrary to the facts, and lacked legal basis. Therefore, the appellee requested that the second instance court dismiss the appeal and uphold the original judgment.

After cross-examination during the second instance, this Court confirmed the main facts found by the original trial court. Additionally, it was found that: Article 4, Paragraph 2 of the 2002 Barter Agreement stipulated: "After Party A completes the preparation of the edible alcohol, it shall notify Party B in writing to take delivery. Party B shall take delivery within 30 days after receiving Party A's notice. If Party B delays in taking delivery, Party A has the right to dispose of the prepared goods otherwise, and Party A shall not be liable for any resulting delay in delivery." Article 5 stipulated: "The edible alcohol to be bartered to Party B shall be collected by Party B from the alcohol production factory warehouse (No. 55 Xinjian Road, Wuwei City, Gansu Province). Party A shall provide assistance. Transportation costs and the risk of cargo damage during transportation shall be borne by Party B."

During the second instance hearing, Gansu Huangtai presented two new pieces of evidence to the Court: (1) the 2002 inventory ledger of Beijing Huangtai, intended to prove that Beijing Huangtai did not receive the liquor delivered by Jianhao Investment. (2) the 1998 Agreement between Huangtai (Party A) and Jianhao Industry (Party B), the invoice stubs for liquor purchased by Jianhao Industry from Gansu Huangtai under that Agreement, and a detailed list of receipts from Zhang Bingfeng and Su Yu. The Agreement stipulated: "1. Party B agrees to lend Party A RMB 7.12 million as listing expenses. Among them, RMB 2 million shall be lent in 1998; RMB 2.4 million in 1999; and RMB 2.72 million in 2000. The three IOUs are part of this Agreement. 2. Party B agrees that Party A may repay Party B's loan with Huangtai series liquor (139 Jin Huangtai at RMB 60 per jin, 20 tons, worth RMB 2.4 million; 59 Jin Huangtai at RMB 30 per jin, 60 tons, worth RMB 3.6 million; Silver Huangtai at RMB 28 per jin, 20 tons, worth RMB 1.12 million, total RMB 7.12 million), or repay the loan with interest (interest calculated at the bank loan rate for the same period) after listing." Based on the prices stipulated in this Agreement, the liquor prices specified in the Agreement and invoices, and the variety and quantity of liquor in the receipts from Zhang Bingfeng and Su Yu, it was intended to prove that the value of the Huangtai series liquor delivered by Jianhao Investment as reflected in the receipts was only RMB 4,328,340.

Regarding the above new evidence, Shi Wenpei did not recognize the authenticity of evidence (1), the 2002 Beijing Huangtai inventory ledger, on the grounds that it was a ledger of Beijing Huangtai itself, and since Gansu Huangtai and Beijing Huangtai were related parties, there was no third party to verify its objective authenticity. Shi Wenpei had no objection to the authenticity of evidence (2), the Agreement, acknowledging that the parties might have signed that agreement at the time. However, he did not recognize the calculation of the liquor prices based on the relevant invoices and the variety and quantity in the receipts, on the grounds that the Barter Agreement was signed against the background of the Agreement, and the prices therein were determined by the parties after inventory. The evidence already cross-examined in the first instance and the correspondence between the parties showed that Gansu Huangtai and Beijing Huangtai had raised no objection on this issue.

This Court held that regarding evidence (1) submitted by Gansu Huangtai, the 2002 Beijing Huangtai inventory ledger, since it was the inventory ledger of Beijing Huangtai, which had a relationship with Gansu Huangtai, and no third party could prove its objective authenticity, and in particular, the first instance had already found through cross-examination that from September 13 to September 20, 2002, Beijing Huangtai received "Jin Huangtai" liquor and issued receipts to Jianhao Industry. Therefore, the ledger produced by Beijing Huangtai itself was insufficient to rebut the above factual evidence. Hence, this Court did not accept this evidence. Regarding evidence (2), the Agreement, since Shi Wenpei had no objection to its authenticity, and the Barter Agreement, which was the basis of the creditor-debtor relationship between the parties, explicitly stated at its beginning: "Party A and Party B signed an Agreement in 1998, under which Party B purchased from Party A 'Jin Huangtai' and 'Silver Huangtai' liquor worth RMB 7 million. Party A has delivered all the goods to Party B, and Party B has paid the full amount...", this Court accepted the authenticity of the Agreement. Regarding the authenticity of the liquor prices specified in the relevant invoices and the variety and quantity of liquor in the receipts in evidence (2), since Shi Wenpei did not provide counter-evidence to prove the invoices were false, and the detailed list of receipts from Zhang Bingfeng and Su Yu was completely consistent with the variety and quantity of liquor in the 16 receipts that Shi Wenpei relied on to claim continued performance of the barter agreement, although Shi Wenpei disputed the calculation method in this evidence, he could not deny the authenticity of the evidence itself. Therefore, this Court accepted the authenticity of evidence (2).

This Court held that the issues in dispute in this case were threefold: First, whether there was a succession relationship between Jianhao Investment and Jianhao Industry, and whether Shi Wenpei was a proper party to the litigation. Second, whether Jianhao Investment had performed its barter obligation, and whether the value of the bartered liquor delivered was RMB 6,499,500 or RMB 4,328,340. Third, whether Gansu Huangtai had breached the contract and whether the liquidated damages were excessive.

Regarding the issue of whether there was a succession relationship between Jianhao Investment and Jianhao Industry and whether Shi Wenpei was a proper party to the litigation, this Court held: Among the evidence already cross-examined and admitted in the first instance, the Certificate issued by the Beijing Administration for Industry and Commerce in 2001 stated: "Beijing Jianhao Industry Company was approved by this Bureau in December 2001 to change its name to Beijing Jianhao Investment Group Co., Ltd." The Enterprise Restructuring Registration Book prepared by the Beijing Administration for Industry and Commerce clearly recorded: Beijing Jianhao Industry Company was restructured as a whole and renamed as Beijing Jianhao Investment Group Co., Ltd. Since Gansu Huangtai only raised a theoretical view that the nature of the name change was not a restructuring but a new establishment, and did not provide evidence that the registration by the Beijing Administration for Industry and Commerce was irregular or erroneous, whether viewed from the constitutive or declaratory effect of enterprise industrial and commercial registration, it could be determined that there was a legal succession relationship between Jianhao Investment and Jianhao Industry. Therefore, Jianhao Investment had the right to demand that Gansu Huangtai perform its obligations under the Barter Agreement. At the same time, Jianhao Investment assigned the above creditor's rights to Shi Wenpei and performed the notification obligation to Gansu Huangtai, which complied with Article 80 of the Contract Law. Therefore, Shi Wenpei naturally had the right to assert claims against Gansu Huangtai. Hence, the first instance's determination that "there was a succession relationship between Jianhao Investment and Jianhao Industry, and Shi Wenpei was a proper party to this litigation" was correct, and this Court upholds it.

Regarding the issue of whether Jianhao Investment had performed its barter obligation and whether the value of the bartered liquor delivered was RMB 6,499,500 or RMB 4,328,340, this Court held: In view of the fact that the 2002 Beijing Huangtai Inventory Ledger, submitted by Gansu Huangtai to prove that Beijing Huangtai did not receive the liquor delivered by Jianhao Investment, was not accepted by this Court, and that in the correspondence between Gansu Huangtai and Jianhao Investment, no objection was raised regarding Jianhao Investment's delivery of the bartered liquor, and in particular, Zhang Bingfeng and Su Yu of Beijing Huangtai issued 16 receipts for the receipt of liquor to Jianhao Investment, it should be determined that Jianhao Investment had performed its barter obligation. Gansu Huangtai's claim that Jianhao Investment had not performed its barter obligation lacked factual basis, and this Court dismisses it. Further, whether the value of the bartered liquor already delivered by Jianhao Investment was RMB 4,999,500 or RMB 4,328,340 became a major issue of dispute between the parties in this case. This Court held: In determining the value of the bartered liquor already delivered by Jianhao Investment, consideration should be given to the intrinsic connection between the 2002 Barter Agreement and the 1998 Agreement, the terms of the agreements, and the process of performance by the parties. Based on the basic content of the Agreement and the Barter Agreement, it could be determined that there was once a loan relationship of RMB 7.12 million between Gansu Huangtai and Jianhao Industry, and Gansu Huangtai repaid the loan to Jianhao Industry with Huangtai series liquor worth RMB 7 million, which took the form of a sale and purchase of Huangtai series liquor. This was confirmed by the statement at the beginning of the Barter Agreement: "Party A and Party B signed an Agreement in 1998, under which Party B purchased from Party A 'Jin Huangtai' and 'Silver Huangtai' liquor worth RMB 7 million. Party A has delivered all the goods to Party B, and Party B has paid the full amount in cash." Against this background and premise, based on their friendly cooperative relationship, the parties reached a new barter arrangement for the aforementioned Huangtai series liquor not yet sold by Jianhao Industry to be exchanged for edible alcohol and wine from Gansu Huangtai, resulting in the Barter Agreement in this case. During the second instance, although Gansu Huangtai produced a detailed list of 16 receipts for Huangtai series liquor from Zhang Bingfeng and Su Yu (the detailed list of receipts was consistent with the quantity of liquor in the 16 receipts already cross-examined in the first instance), and calculated, based on the Huangtai series liquor prices in the 1998 Agreement, that the value of the Huangtai series liquor delivered by Jianhao Investment as reflected in the 16 receipts was RMB 4,328,340, it should be noted that the Huangtai series liquor prices stipulated in the 1998 Agreement were determined for the purpose of Gansu Huangtai repaying its RMB 7.12 million debt to Jianhao Industry with liquor, and were not specifically stipulated for the new 2002 Barter Agreement signed after the loan relationship had been settled between the parties in 2002. The 2002 Barter Agreement did not stipulate the unit price of the bartered liquor, but clearly stipulated the total value of the bartered liquor in Articles 1 and 3: "After both Party A and Party B jointly conduct an inventory of the warehouse of Party B, it is determined that the value of the bartered liquor is RMB 6,499,500." "Both parties agree that the quantities of edible alcohol and wine to be exchanged are: 75,000 bottles of Huangtai dry red wine, worth RMB 1.5 million; 1,111 tons of premium edible alcohol, worth RMB 4,999,500." This stipulation should be interpreted as the parties not being concerned with the unit price of the bartered liquor, but focusing on determining the total value of the bartered liquor. Although the same Huangtai series liquor was involved, because the purposes of the 1998 Agreement and the 2002 Barter Agreement were different, and because over time, the price of liquor would change with market supply and demand, Gansu Huangtai's static and mechanical reliance on the unit liquor price stipulated in the 1998 Agreement (which was for the purpose of repayment) to calculate the value of the bartered liquor in the 2002 Barter Agreement (which was for the purpose of barter) not only violated the laws of market value, but also contravened the purposes of the above two agreements, and more specifically, clearly violated the explicit stipulations on the value of the bartered liquor in Articles 1 and 3 of the 2002 Barter Agreement. Therefore, this Court determines that the parties had clearly confirmed the value of the bartered liquor as RMB 6,499,500. Gansu Huangtai's claim that the value of the liquor paid by Jianhao Investment was only RMB 4,328,340, not the RMB 6,499,500 stipulated in the Barter Agreement, was unfounded, and this Court does not support it.

Regarding the issue of whether Gansu Huangtai breached the contract and whether the liquidated damages were excessively high, this Court holds that: Although Article 4, paragraph 2 of the 2002 Barter Agreement expressly provides that "Party A shall, after completing the stocking of edible alcohol, notify Party B in writing to take delivery; Party B shall take delivery within 30 days of Party A's notice. If Party B delays taking delivery, Party A has the right to otherwise dispose of the stocked goods, and Party A shall not be liable for any delay in delivery caused thereby," and Article 5 of the same agreement has already made clear provisions on the method of bartering edible alcohol, i.e., "the edible alcohol bartered to Party B shall be collected by Party B from the warehouse of the alcohol manufacturer (No. 55 Xinjian Road, Wuwei City, Gansu Province), with Party A providing assistance, and the transportation costs and risk of cargo damage during transport shall be borne by Party B," nevertheless, as evidenced by the letter dated May 12, 2003 from Jianhao Industry to Gansu Huangtai stating "Our side has prepared to receive the alcohol; please contact us as soon as possible regarding delivery arrangements," and the two replies from Gansu Huangtai to Jianhao Industry dated May 16, 2003 and June 7, 2003, stating "In view of the impact of the current SARS epidemic, the transportation of edible goods is restricted, coupled with difficulties in allocating specialized railway tank cars, we cannot deliver the goods to your side on schedule; after the epidemic situation eases, we will deliver the goods in full to your company" and "We have received your letter of June 2 entitled 'Further Letter to Huangtai Liquor on the Issue of Alcohol Delivery'. Because railway regulations do not permit the consignment of flammable and explosive goods, our company cannot meet your requirement for delivery of alcohol by railway transportation," it should be determined that the parties have changed the method of performance for the barter of edible alcohol, and Gansu Huangtai is obligated to deliver the goods to Jianhao Investment. In particular, Article 4, paragraph 1 of the 2002 Barter Agreement expressly provides that "Party A shall deliver all the wine on the day of transferring the liquor inventory, and shall pay off the edible alcohol before December 31, 2003. If Party A fails to deliver the alcohol within this time limit, it shall pay liquidated damages at a rate of 0.04% per day on the value of the delayed goods." From the content of a series of replies from Gansu Huangtai to Jianhao Investment between May 31 and July 17, 2004, Gansu Huangtai appears to have delayed or even refused to perform its obligation to barter edible alcohol. Therefore, this Court holds that: Since Gansu Huangtai has still not delivered the edible alcohol to date, pursuant to the provision of Article 4, paragraph 1 of the Barter Agreement that "Gansu Huangtai shall pay off the edible alcohol before December 31, 2003," it should be determined that Gansu Huangtai has breached the contract and shall pay liquidated damages as agreed. As to whether the agreed liquidated damages are excessively high, the liquidated damages system established by Article 114 of the Contract Law has determined that liquidated damages have a dual nature of "compensation and punishment." Paragraph 2 of that Article of the Contract Law clearly provides that "if the agreed liquidated damages are excessively higher than the losses caused, a party may request the people's court or an arbitration institution to make an appropriate reduction." According to this, it should be interpreted that only in cases where the liquidated damages are "excessively higher than the losses caused" can they be appropriately adjusted, while it is unnecessary to adjust in cases of ordinary excess. Given that Gansu Huangtai has breached the contract in this case and is suspected of maliciously delaying or even refusing to perform, and there is no evidence proving that the daily rate of 0.04% is excessively high, the daily rate of 0.04% as stipulated in the Barter Agreement cannot be considered excessively high. Gansu Huangtai's arguments that it did not breach the contract and should not pay liquidated damages, and that the liquidated damages are excessively high and should be reduced, are unfounded and are rejected by this Court. The first-instance court's judgment that Gansu Huangtai should pay Shi Wenpei liquidated damages of RMB 2,099,790 is correct, and this Court affirms it.

In conclusion, this Court holds that: The first-instance judgment found the facts basically clearly and applied the law correctly. Pursuant to Article 153, paragraph 1, item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, this Court hereby adjudicates as follows:

The appeal is dismissed and the original judgment is affirmed.

The litigation acceptance fee at first instance of RMB 78,012 and the preservation fee of RMB 5,000, totaling RMB 83,012, shall be executed in accordance with the original judgment; the litigation acceptance fee at second instance of RMB 78,012 shall be borne by Gansu Huangtai Brewing (Group) Co., Ltd.

This judgment is final.
